notes.meaning: Gaal boasts before the crowd that if he were in charge, he would quickly drive Abimelech out of power. Feeling confident, he openly dares Abimelech to gather his army and come out to fight. Gaal uses smooth, proud talk to win over the people and set himself up as their new leader.

Zebul was the city ruler whom Abimelech had placed in charge of Shechem. When he hears Gaal bragging and threatening Abimelech, he becomes furious. He realizes Gaal is trying to take away his authority and steal the city.

Zebul hides his anger for the moment and secretly sends messengers to Abimelech. He warns the king that Gaal and his family have moved into Shechem and are turning the citizens against him. This secret report gives Abimelech time to plan before the rebels realize what is happening.

Zebul sends Abimelech practical military advice on how to handle the rebellion. He tells him to bring his troops under the cover of darkness and hide in the open fields near the city. This surprise move would keep the city from preparing a proper defense.

Zebul explains the rest of the trap: Abimelech should strike the city right at sunrise. When Gaal rushes out with his fighters to meet him, Abimelech can attack them in the open before they can organize. A quick, decisive counterattack would crush the rebellion before it grows.

Abimelech follows the plan and marches his troops out during the night. He divides his army into four groups and hides them near Shechem. Dividing the men allowed him to surround the approaches to the city from several sides.

Gaal wakes up early and walks out to stand at the entrance of the city gate, keeping watch over the area. Just as he steps outside, Abimelech and his soldiers emerge from their hiding spots. The trap is sprung before Gaal even knows he is in danger.

Gaal spots figures moving along the mountain ridges and tells Zebul that people are marching down. Zebul pretends everything is fine and tells him he is only seeing the shadows cast by the mountains in the early morning light. By making Gaal doubt his own eyes, Zebul buys Abimelech precious minutes to get closer.

Gaal looks again and knows he is not imagining things. He shouts that troops are pouring down from the high center of the land, with another unit marching past the Diviners' Oak. The enemy forces are closing in from multiple directions at once.

Now that Abimelech is at the gate, Zebul drops his friendly act and mocks Gaal. He asks where Gaal's proud bragging has gone, reminding him how he had laughed at Abimelech only days before. Zebul dares him to step outside and fight the very men he ridiculed.

With his pride on the line before the watching citizens, Gaal has no choice but to take the field. He gathers his men and leads the fighters of Shechem out of the gate to face Abimelech. What began as reckless bragging now turns into real bloodshed.

Abimelech quickly overpowers Gaal's forces and chases them across the field. Gaal runs for his life back toward the safety of the city. Many of his fighters fall wounded or dead all along the path right up to the gate.

Abimelech pulls back and sets up camp at the nearby town of Arumah, waiting to see what Shechem will do next. Back inside the city, Zebul uses Gaal's embarrassing defeat to drive him and his relatives out of town completely. Gaal's brief bid for power collapses in disgrace.

The next morning, the people of Shechem walk out into the open fields, likely thinking the danger has passed with Gaal gone. They probably went out to work on their harvest or tend their crops. Word quickly reaches Abimelech that the citizens are outside their defensive walls.

other.view: Some scholars view verses 42–49 as a second, independent account of the attack on Shechem that was later joined with the earlier story.

notes.meaning: Abimelech splits his army into three groups and sets a fresh ambush in the fields. When he sees the unarmed citizens working outside, he and his men leap out and attack them without warning. His cruelty shows he is interested in revenge, not just restoring order.

Abimelech leads his group straight to the city gate to block the entrance so nobody can run back inside for safety. Meanwhile, the other two companies sweep through the fields and cut down the helpless workers. No one in the open fields is allowed to escape.

Abimelech battles against Shechem all through the day until he breaches the defenses and captures it. He slaughters the inhabitants, levels every building to the ground, and scatters salt across the ruins. Spreading salt was a symbolic act showing he wanted the city to remain a barren, ruined wasteland forever.

notes.meaning: When the leaders living in the fortified tower of Shechem hear about the city's destruction, they flee into the stronghold of the temple of El-berith. They hoped their pagan idol would protect them from Abimelech's wrath. Turning to false gods for safety only leads people into a trap.

Spies quickly report to Abimelech that the remaining leaders of Shechem are packed inside that temple stronghold. Knowing where his enemies are gathered gives him the chance to wipe them out all at once. His thirst for vengeance will not stop until every rival is dead.

Abimelech leads his soldiers up Mount Zalmon, a wooded mountain near the city. He grabs an axe, chops off a heavy tree branch, and carries it on his own shoulder. He then orders his men to work fast and copy exactly what they saw him do.

Every soldier cuts a branch and carries it down behind Abimelech. They pile the wood around the base of the stronghold and set the building on fire, suffocating and burning about a thousand men and women inside. In this terrible way, Jotham's warning that fire would come out from the bramble came true.

Next, Abimelech marches northeast to the town of Thebez, surrounds it, and captures it. Thebez was likely allied with Shechem in the revolt against him. Even after destroying Shechem, Abimelech's rage drives him to keep conquering.

Inside Thebez stood a strong, fortified tower where all the surviving men, women, and leaders fled for refuge. They bolted the heavy gates shut behind them and climbed up to the flat roof. This high tower was their last line of defense against the invaders.

Abimelech presses his attack right up to the tower itself, determined to break through. He walks directly up to the wooden entrance to set it on fire, expecting to repeat the slaughter he carried out at Shechem. His past success makes him reckless and overconfident.

As Abimelech reaches the door, a woman on the roof drops a heavy upper millstone straight onto his head. The stone cracks his skull and leaves him dying on the ground. God brought fitting justice upon him, because Abimelech had murdered his seventy brothers upon a stone.

Realizing he is dying, Abimelech urgently calls his armor-bearer and orders the young man to finish him with a sword. In that ancient culture, it was considered a humiliating disgrace for a mighty warrior to be killed by a woman. Even with his final breath, Abimelech cares more about his pride than about making peace with God.

When the Israelite soldiers see that their commander is dead, the whole campaign falls apart. Without Abimelech to lead them, they pack up and return to their homes. His violent kingdom ends as quickly as it began.

This tragic ending shows how God repaid Abimelech for the evil crime he committed against his father’s household. He had ruthlessly murdered his seventy half-brothers to seize a crown that was not his. God's justice may seem slow, but no sinner can escape it in the end.

God also brought the wickedness of the leaders of Shechem right back onto their own heads. Because they had funded and supported the murder of Gideon's family, they perished by the very tyrant they helped make king. The curse spoken by Jotham was fulfilled down to the last detail.
